claims.text: The local electronic structure of a transition-metal single-atom site governs ORR catalytic activity.
The local electronic structure of a transition-metal single-atom site governs ORR selectivity.
The local electronic structure of a transition-metal single-atom site governs ORR durability.
Nearby heteroatom dopants modulate the electron density of the metal active site.
Nitrogen is a stronger electron donor to the metal site than boron or phosphorus in the proposed carbon-supported catalysts.
Stronger electron-donating dopants increase electron density at the metal center.
Greater electron density at the metal center lowers the activation energy for oxygen reduction.
Lowering the ORR activation energy improves catalytic activity.
Increasing electron density at the metal center improves ORR selectivity.
Stronger electron donation stabilizes the single-atom active site.
Stabilization of the active site improves catalyst durability.
Nitrogen-doped supports will produce higher ORR current densities than less electron-donating boron- or phosphorus-doped supports.
Nitrogen-doped supports will produce lower ORR onset potentials than less electron-donating boron- or phosphorus-doped supports.
Nitrogen-doped supports will give better long-term stability than less electron-donating boron- or phosphorus-doped supports.
The proposed dopant–electronic-structure relationship is expected to hold for single-atom ORR catalysts in acidic environments.
The proposed relationship may not extend to other catalytic reactions or catalyst architectures.
Metal loading, atomic-site distribution, synthesis variation, and multifactor interactions may affect the quantitative performance differences.
